question.prompt: Raashan, Sylvia, and Ted play the following game. Each starts with \(\$1.\) A bell rings every \(15\) seconds, at which time each of the players who currently have money simultaneously chooses one of the other two players independently and at random and gives \(\$1\) to that player. What is the probability that after the bell has rung \(2019\) times, each player will have \(\$1?\) (For example, Raashan and Ted may each decide to give \(\$1\) to Sylvia, and Sylvia may decide to give her dollar to Ted, at which point Raashan will have \(\$0,\) Sylvia will have \(\$2,\) and Ted will have \(\$1,\) and that is the end of the first round of play. In the second round Raashan has no money to give, but Sylvia and Ted might choose each other to give their \(\$1\) to, and the holdings will be the same at the end of the second round.)

solutions.title: Compare the two money distributions
solutions.explanation:
The key is to examine the possible money distributions before just one round. The total stays at 3 dollars, and nobody can finish a round with all 3: a player who starts with money sends a dollar that finishes with someone else, while a player who starts with none can receive at most two dollars. Thus, up to relabeling the players, the only states are \((1,1,1)\) and \((2,1,0)\).

Suppose a round starts at \((1,1,1)\). If Raashan gives to Sylvia, then Sylvia already receives one dollar, so Ted must give to Raashan. Sylvia must then give to Ted. Those two required choices are independent, giving probability
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14.
\]
If Raashan instead gives to Ted, the same reasoning gives probability \(\frac14\).

Now suppose Raashan has 2 dollars, Sylvia has 1, and Ted has 0. After giving, Raashan keeps one dollar, so Sylvia must avoid giving to him and must give to Ted. Raashan must then give to Sylvia. Again, the probability is
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14.
\]
Relabeling the players does not change this calculation.

Therefore every possible starting state gives a \(\frac14\) chance of ending the next round with one dollar each. If \(p\) is the probability that round 2019 starts in state \((1,1,1)\), the desired probability is
\[
p\cdot\frac14+(1-p)\cdot\frac14=\boxed{\frac14}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
